item: T4.6 — Low-thrust and higher-fidelity mission design (mention-only) and a fidelity ladder
summary:
## Why electric propulsion breaks the Lambert model

Chemical propulsion (Isp ~300-450 s) delivers a lot of thrust briefly — you can treat a burn as an instantaneous velocity change (an "impulse"), which is exactly what makes Lambert's problem the right tool: given two positions and a time of flight, solve for the connecting Kepler arc, and the delta-v is just the vector difference between the arc's endpoint velocities and the planets' velocities. Electric propulsion (ion, Hall-effect) inverts the trade: Isp of 1,500-4,100+ s (much better propellant efficiency) but thrust of only tens to a couple hundred millinewtons, because thrust is limited by onboard electrical power, not by how fast you can burn chemical energy. NASA's Dawn spacecraft is the canonical example: its NSTAR ion engine ran at 2.3 kW, produced only ~92 mN of thrust, but at Isp ~3,100 s it accumulated close to 11 km/s of total delta-v over the mission — several times what a chemical stage of similar mass could deliver (Wikipedia "Electric propulsion"; NASA ion-propulsion fact sheet via search, not opened directly).

Because the thrust is continuous and tiny relative to spacecraft weight, you cannot approximate a low-thrust maneuver as an instantaneous impulse — burns last hours to months, and the trajectory during the burn is neither a clean ellipse nor a clean hyperbola. This turns trajectory design into an **optimal control problem**: find a time-varying control (thrust direction and duty cycle) u(t) that satisfies the equations of motion and the boundary conditions while minimizing propellant use or flight time. There is no closed-form solution in general (unlike two-body Keplerian motion), so it must be solved numerically. Two families of numerical method exist: **indirect methods** apply Pontryagin's Minimum Principle to derive costate equations analytically, turning the problem into a two-point boundary-value problem solved by shooting; **indirect methods are more mathematically elegant but brutally sensitive to the initial guess**. **Direct methods** instead discretize the whole trajectory into a finite set of decision variables and hand the resulting large nonlinear program (NLP) to a general solver (SNOPT, IPOPT); this is what essentially every practical mission-design tool uses today because it tolerates poor initial guesses far better.

## The Sims-Flanagan transcription

The standard direct-transcription recipe for low-thrust legs, used by pykep, JPL's MALTO, and NASA Goddard's EMTG, is the **Sims-Flanagan transcription** (I could not open pykep's simsflanagan doc page directly — both esa.github.io and the raw GitHub .rst 404'd this session — so this is reconstructed from WebSearch snippets quoting the page, confidence "likely" not "verified"):

- Chop a leg (departure body to arrival body) into N equal-duration **segments**.
- Approximate the continuous thrust in each segment by a single **bounded impulsive delta-v** applied at the segment's midpoint (a "control node"); the spacecraft coasts on an ordinary two-body Kepler arc between impulses. This is the key trick — it turns "solve for a continuous control history" into "solve for N discrete throttle vectors," which is exactly the kind of finite-dimensional problem an NLP solver eats.
- Propagate forward in time from the departure state and backward in time from the arrival state; the two propagations must agree in position, velocity, and mass at a **mid-leg match point** — these agreement conditions become nonlinear equality constraints in the NLP.
- Mass decreases at each impulse per the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation (Δm from Δv and Isp).
- Decision variables per leg: departure/arrival epochs (or leg duration) plus N throttle vectors (3 components each, magnitude ≤ 1, scaled by max thrust/Isp).

EMTG calls this mode "MGALT" and also offers a higher-fidelity mode called "FBLT" that does true forward/backward numerical integration with piecewise-constant control rather than the segment-Kepler approximation — a further fidelity step above Sims-Flanagan itself. EMTG couples the NLP (SNOPT) with a global-search heuristic (Monotonic Basin Hopping) to escape local minima, and can pull SPICE ephemerides plus detailed thruster/power/launch-vehicle models (WebSearch summaries of EMTG docs and an NTRS technical paper — not opened directly).

pykep (ESA's library, built for GTOC-class problems) is the natural long-term dependency if the project ever adds a low-thrust mode: it already has both impulsive Lambert-arc legs and Sims-Flanagan low-thrust legs, Izzo's fast Lambert solver, ephemerides, and a `trajopt` module of pre-built problem classes. The master document already flags that WASM-compiling pykep (C++/Boost) is painful for a browser deployment — so a thin server-side service (rather than in-browser optimization) is the likely path if this is ever built, and it should be scoped as a distinct future phase, not folded into the v1 Lambert/porkchop work.

## The fidelity ladder (the deliverable this item exists to produce)

Five levels, each answering "what does it compute, what does it ignore, roughly how wrong is it, and what should the UI say."

**Level 0 — Two-body Keplerian (teaching).** Computes position/velocity from the 6 classical elements via Kepler's equation around a single point-mass body; no perturbations at all. Ignores drag, J2, third-body, SRP — everything. This mode is *for* showing the idealized ellipse, so "error vs reality" isn't really the right lens — a real LEO satellite will visibly diverge (degrees of mean anomaly per day) from its own two-body prediction, and that's expected, not a bug. Disclosure: *"Idealized two-body orbit for teaching — not a real satellite's actual path."*

**Level 1 — SGP4 catalog (real Earth satellites).** Computes TEME position/velocity from published TLE mean elements via SGP4/SDP4, converted to ECEF/geodetic. Ignores any maneuvers since the TLE epoch and any dynamics beyond what SGP4's built-in drag model encodes. Accuracy degrades with TLE staleness (order of single-digit km per day for LEO, worse for drag-dominated objects) — Track 2 should hold the authoritative citation for the exact figure; flagged here only as a cross-check. Disclosure: *"Real satellite position from published TLE data (epoch shown); accuracy degrades the further from that epoch we are."*

**Level 2 — Impulsive patched-conic Lambert transfers (this project's v1 interplanetary layer).** Computes one Lambert solve per (departure date, arrival date) pair: a heliocentric two-body Kepler arc between planet ephemeris positions, with v∞ excess velocities at each planet's sphere of influence summed into a delta-v (departure C3, arrival v∞). Ignores finite burn duration, capture-orbit insertion cost, precise plane-change cost when the transfer plane isn't quite the target's actual plane, n-body perturbations during the coast, and launch-vehicle-specific C3-vs-payload curves. The heliocentric-leg delta-v itself is typically within a few percent of a real mission's reported number for that leg, but *total* mission delta-v is understated because capture/insertion and margin are omitted. Disclosure: *"Idealized impulsive (instant-burn) transfer using patched-conic Lambert arcs. Departure and arrival delta-v shown are v-infinity excess speeds at each planet's sphere of influence — capture-orbit insertion, plane-change, and launch-vehicle-specific costs are not included."*

**Level 3 — Finite burns / n-body / capture spirals / plane changes / launch-vehicle C3 curves.** Computes real finite-duration burns with gravity losses, n-body or CR3BP propagation instead of patched conics, explicit capture-insertion delta-v, explicit plane-change cost, and matches departure C3 against an actual launch vehicle's performance curve. This is roughly GMAT/STK-grade fidelity for chemical-propulsion missions — still no continuous low-thrust, no navigation/uncertainty. Disclosure: *"Higher-fidelity model including capture burns, plane changes, and n-body dynamics — flight-project-grade for chemical-propulsion missions, but still assumes impulsive burns."*

**Level 4 — Low-thrust, navigation, uncertainty (mention-only, out of scope through v2).** This is where Sims-Flanagan / FBLT-style direct transcription solved with an NLP (as in pykep/EMTG/MALTO) lives, plus orbit-determination/navigation covariance propagation for real mission ops. Not modeled by this project at all in the current roadmap. Disclosure: *"Not modeled. Electric-propulsion (low-thrust) missions, precise navigation, and uncertainty quantification are outside this tool's scope; results here apply only to chemical/impulsive-burn missions."*

## Worked numbers computed this session

Synodic period formula: T_syn = 1/|1/T1 − 1/T2|, where T1, T2 are sidereal orbital periods. Using T_earth=365.256 d, T_venus=224.701 d, T_mars=686.980 d, T_jupiter=4332.59 d, computed in `notes/t4_6_compute.py`:
- Earth–Venus: **583.92 days**
- Earth–Mars: **779.93 days** (matches the ~780-day anchor already in the master doc)
- Earth–Jupiter: **398.88 days** — shorter than Earth-Mars despite Jupiter being much farther out, because Jupiter's own period is so long that 1/T_jupiter is nearly negligible, so T_syn approaches Earth's own period (365 d) from above; the cadence is set by the *difference* of angular rates, not by which body is "faster."

Also computed the idealized (coplanar, tangential-burn, Hohmann-limit) Earth→Mars transfer to connect the Lambert/porkchop chain: v_earth_circ=29.78 km/s, v_mars_circ=24.13 km/s, transfer-orbit perihelion speed=32.73 km/s, transfer-orbit aphelion speed=21.48 km/s → v∞_departure=2.95 km/s, v∞_arrival=2.65 km/s, time-of-flight=258.9 days (~8.6 months). This is the Lambert special case at minimum energy; a general (non-optimal-date) Lambert solve across a porkchop grid gives higher v∞ sums, consistent with the master doc's stated "good real-window" anchor of ~5.6–6 km/s total.

## Pitfalls / how this maps to the professor's lecture and the project phases

- Don't let "add low-thrust" sneak into v1/C1 scope — it requires a different solver stack (NLP + direct transcription) and different graph-edge semantics, not an extension of the Lambert-based edge model. One paragraph in the proposal is the right amount of coverage: the graph-edge abstraction (node = body/window, edge = transfer with vector cost) is *compatible* with a future low-thrust edge type computed via Sims-Flanagan, but v1 edges are impulsive Lambert only.

key_facts.fact: Because thrust is continuous and tiny relative to spacecraft weight, low-thrust trajectories cannot be modeled as instantaneous velocity impulses (the Lambert-problem assumption); trajectory design becomes an optimal-control problem with no closed-form solution, solved numerically via indirect (Pontryagin/costate shooting) or direct (finite-dimensional NLP) transcription.

key_facts.fact: Sims-Flanagan transcription: chop a low-thrust leg into N equal-duration segments, replace continuous thrust in each with one bounded impulsive delta-v at the segment midpoint, coast on Kepler arcs between impulses; propagate forward from departure and backward from arrival, require the two to match at a mid-leg point (position/velocity/mass) as NLP equality constraints; mass updates via Tsiolkovsky. Decision variables: epochs plus N throttle vectors.
key_facts.source: WebSearch summary quoting esa/pykep simsflanagan docs (page itself 404'd on direct fetch)

key_facts.fact: Sims-Flanagan is the shared backbone of JPL's MALTO and NASA Goddard's EMTG (EMTG's 'MGALT' mode); EMTG also has a higher-fidelity 'FBLT' mode with true forward/backward numerical integration instead of the segment-Kepler approximation, and couples the NLP with SNOPT plus Monotonic Basin Hopping for global search, using SPICE ephemerides and launch-vehicle/thruster/power models.

This deserves exactly one paragraph in the v1 proposal: the graph-edge abstraction (node=body/window, edge=transfer with vector cost) is compatible with a future low-thrust edge type, but v1 edges are impulsive Lambert only. The fidelity ladder (Level 0 teaching Keplerian, Level 1 SGP4 catalog, Level 2 impulsive patched-conic Lambert = v1's interplanetary layer, Level 3 finite-burn/n-body/capture/launch-vehicle-C3, Level 4 low-thrust/nav/uncertainty = out of scope) is the concrete deliverable the professor will want, and should likely become an actual UI element (a fidelity-level badge with tooltip disclosure text, given verbatim per level above) rather than only README prose — directly answers Track 3's requirement to document "what real mission design includes that v1 will honestly omit."

question_inputs.question: Which fidelity shortcuts are acceptable for a v1 (impulsive burns only, patched conics, ignore capture spirals, planar assumptions) and how should the UI disclose them? Give a fidelity ladder and disclosure wording.
question_inputs.answer: v1 should sit at Level 2 of the 5-level ladder (impulsive patched-conic Lambert transfers): one Lambert solve per date pair, delta-v reported as summed v-infinity at each SOI, no capture-spiral cost, no launch-vehicle C3 curve, simplified plane-change handling. This matches essentially every public porkchop tool (including NASA's Trajectory Browser), so it's well-precedented for v1 — but must ship with explicit disclosure text (given per-level in the summary/project_relevance above) and ideally a visible fidelity-level badge (0 teaching Keplerian / 1 SGP4 catalog / 2 patched-conic Lambert / 3 finite-burn n-body / 4 low-thrust+nav, out of scope) so users see which level produced any given number. Low-thrust (Level 4) is explicitly mention-only — it needs a different solver (Sims-Flanagan + NLP), not an extension of the Lambert graph-edge model.

question_inputs.question: Given two dates, what exactly does one Lambert solve return, and how do its v-infinity values become the delta-v numbers on a porkchop? Walk through the full chain with formulas and one worked Earth-to-Mars example.
question_inputs.answer: A Lambert solve takes r1 (departure position), r2 (arrival position), and time-of-flight, and returns the transfer arc's velocities v1, v2. v_inf_departure = |v1 - v_earth(t_dep)|, v_inf_arrival = |v2 - v_mars(t_arr)|; C3 = v_inf_dep^2 is the launch-energy metric on porkchop departure axes. Worked idealized Hohmann-limit example (notes/t4_6_compute.py): v_earth_circ=29.78 km/s, v_mars_circ=24.13 km/s, transfer perihelion/aphelion speeds 32.73/21.48 km/s, giving v_inf_dep=2.95 km/s, v_inf_arr=2.65 km/s, ToF=258.9 days. This is the minimum-energy special case; general porkchop-grid Lambert solves at non-optimal dates give higher v_inf sums, consistent with the master doc's ~5.6-6 km/s good-window anchor. (Full Izzo-solver derivation belongs to the dedicated Lambert/porkchop Track-4 item; this is the mechanical chain connecting Lambert output to porkchop delta-v.)

question_inputs.question: Why do launch windows recur, and what sets their cadence per planet pair? Give the synodic period formula and computed values for Earth-Mars, Earth-Venus, Earth-Jupiter.
question_inputs.answer: Launch windows recur because favorable Earth-target relative geometry repeats with the synodic period T_syn = 1/|1/T1 - 1/T2| (T1, T2 = sidereal periods) — the cadence is set by the difference in the two planets' angular rates, not either planet's period alone. Computed (notes/t4_6_compute.py): Earth-Venus=583.92 d, Earth-Mars=779.93 d (matches master doc's ~780 d anchor), Earth-Jupiter=398.88 d — shorter than Earth-Mars despite Jupiter being far more distant, because Jupiter's very long period makes 1/T_jupiter nearly negligible, so T_syn approaches Earth's own ~365-day period from above.
